paragraphs: Friend, here's what I take from this one. Nehemiah hears a crowd crying out, and the ones causing the pain are God's own people. He doesn't look away. He gets extremely angry, thinks it through, and then he speaks up for families who are about to lose everything (Nehemiah 5:6-7). When people around you are hurting and you have the power to help, God's people don't just keep working on the wall.

Now look at what Nehemiah says to the nobles and officials: "What you are doing is not right. Shouldn't you walk in the fear of our God…" (Nehemiah 5:9). And then he says, "Please, let us stop this usury." Not "you," friend, "us" (Nehemiah 5:10). He stands in the same line as the people he corrects. And I tell you, I'd rather be corrected by someone standing next to me than someone pointing at me from across the kitchen!

The best part comes at the end. For twelve years as governor, Nehemiah doesn't take the food allotted to him, "because of my fear of God" (Nehemiah 5:14-15). He could have, and the governors before him did. He gives up what he's owed because the people's burden is so heavy (Nehemiah 5:18). So ask yourself, baker, where can you ease someone's load today? Fearing God looks like that: you do the right thing, and you pour out your own batch for somebody else.
